newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: New refineries seen reshaping MidEast sugar trade.
newsitem.headline: New refineries seen reshaping MidEast sugar trade.

text.p: The recent building of two sugar refineries in the Middle East is seen moulding fresh relationships in the region's sugar trade, said the International Sugar Organisation's (ISO) chief economist.

Tony Hannah of the ISO said at the sugar body's member meeting in Mauritius that the Middle East, a big import market traditionally supplied mainly with beet sugar from the European Union, was now increasingly drawing raw sugar from other areas.
"The raw sugar exporters, particularly Australia and Thailand, are now able to, in a sense, get their sugar into the Mediterranean through these refineries," Hannah told Reuters in an interview.

New refineries have sprung up in Dubai, where the Al Khaleej plant at Jebel Ali has an annual capacity of 720,000 tonnes. Saudi Arabia's Jeddah is home to another with capacity of around 500,000 tonnes.
"In the case of Saudi Arabia they are basically replacing EU and Chinese sugar with locally refined sugar, using mainly Australian raws."
Greater competition between suppliers of different sugars was also becoming evident, he said.

"There you have a direct conflict between beet and cane sugar through these new refineries that are being built there. (Countries supplying) raws have big advantages with these refineries over beet sugar which is bagged and more expensive to transport."
Hannah said that although this shift had implications for EU sugar exports, it was still too early to make an assessment of the extent as the refineries were only starting to come on stream.
An EU official told Reuters on Tuesday that if more new refineries sprung up, it would become a worry for Europe, the world's biggest sugar exporter.
"If this is going to be symptomatic of a more substantial move in the world...then clearly that is going to have implications for world trade," the official said.
